answer.label: Not Zig Ziglar — a widely circulated modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: American self-help author · earliest verifiable version, 1982
answer.sourceLine: Zig Ziglar did use a version of this saying, but he explicitly disclaimed authorship — he credited a “Carl Bard” whose existence and authorship Quote Investigator could not verify ↗. The earliest documented form of the line appears in James R. Sherman’s 1982 book Rejection: “You can’t go back and make a new start, but you can start right now and make a brand new ending.” The exact wording quoted here is a later paraphrase that traces to no specific primary source by Ziglar.

source.heading: The saying’s paper trail

docMeta.dd: Zig Ziglar (also C. S. Lewis, Carl Bard, Maria Robinson)

source.excerpt: You can’t go back and make a new start, but you can start right now and make a brand new ending.
trail: The authoritative investigation is Quote Investigator’s ‘We Cannot Go Back and Start Over’ ↗, which locates the earliest version in James R. Sherman’s 1982 book Rejection.
Per the same source, Zig Ziglar used the saying but disclaimed it — in a 2000 column and his 2003 collection Zig Ziglar’s Life Lifters he credited “Carl Bard,” a name QI could not otherwise verify.
An independent AAP FactCheck ↗ rates the popular C. S. Lewis attribution “False,” and likewise points to Sherman’s 1982 Rejection as the probable source.

The wording drifts across sources — Maria Robinson is credited with “Nobody can go back and start a new beginning, but anyone can start today and make a new ending,” showing how freely this idea is reworded and re-signed.
source.excerptNote: The earliest verifiable form of the saying, from James R. Sherman’s 1982 book Rejection, per Quote Investigator. The quoted wording — “We cannot go back and start over, but we can begin now, and make a new ending” — is one of several later reworkings, not attested in any Ziglar work as his own.

author.name: James R. Sherman
author.heading: About James R. Sherman
author.metaLine: American self-help author · earliest documented form of the saying, 1982
author.bio: James R. Sherman is an American self-help writer whose 1982 book Rejection contains the earliest version of this saying that researchers have located: “You can’t go back and make a new start, but you can start right now and make a brand new ending.” Whether Sherman coined the line or repeated an existing one is not established — but no earlier printed source has been found. The polished modern wording usually pinned on Zig Ziglar or C. S. Lewis is a later reworking of Sherman’s sentence.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: This uplifting one-liner is a floating quotation: the same idea circulates in dozens of wordings, each re-signed with a more famous name. Zig Ziglar is a common signature, but he himself passed the credit along.

items.why: Ziglar did quote the saying — in a 2000 column and his 2003 book Zig Ziglar’s Life Lifters — but he credited it to “Carl Bard,” not himself, per Quote Investigator ↗. Crediting it to Ziglar reverses what he actually did.
Lewis died in 1963 and there is no record of the line in his work; AAP FactCheck ↗ rates the attribution “False.”
The name Ziglar cited; Quote Investigator found no independent evidence that a “Carl Bard” authored it, so this credit simply passes the mystery along one more step.

Robinson is widely credited with “Nobody can go back and start a new beginning, but anyone can start today and make a new ending” — a variant that shows how the ‘make a new ending’ phrasing detaches from any one author.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented version is James R. Sherman’s, in his 1982 book Rejection — not Ziglar’s, not Lewis’s — per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why the wording keeps changing
lead: Sayings like this are what folklorists call ‘floating’ quotations: a memorable thought with no fixed author, restated in fresh words and reattached to whichever famous name feels right. Because no single canonical sentence exists, each retelling drifts — ‘make a new start’ becomes ‘start over,’ ‘brand new ending’ becomes ‘a new ending’ — and the exact form quoted here is just one of many.
That drift is exactly why a confident single-author claim is impossible. The honest answer is a chain of attestation, not a signature.
context.pull: A thought this tidy rarely has one owner — it has a lineage.
